prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator (B012) as my preferred single-part configuration, and round 1 has not moved me off it. The discovery is a specific, checkable chain: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the time-reversal-protected helical edge states, and Molenkamp's group observed quantised edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells, with the nonlocal and size-dependent transport that distinguishes it from trivial edge conduction. More than fifteen years of work by independent groups, using transport, ARPES and STM, have left the interpretation stable. That matters to me as an experimentalist, because the thing being credited is not still being argued about. The chair's summary shows that every proponent of B047 and B019 calls B012 the more mature option or lists it as an alternative, and that six members list it as an alternative; I do not treat those counts as a verdict, but they tell me that B012 is the configuration least likely to be judged unsound by any member on scientific grounds. On the chair's question about the 2016 prize, I treat it as context and not a bar: that prize recognised topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall-type topological phases, whereas the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators, helical edge states without a magnetic field, and their observation in a real material came afterwards and were verified separately. My answer to the chair's question on a fair citation is that it can be worded around what Kane and Mele predicted and what Molenkamp first observed, which is accurate as written; the three-name limit is a statutory constraint and not a statement about who else mattered.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and I do not think it can be fully argued away. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological-insulator work (Fu, Kane and Mele; Moore and Balents; Hsieh and Hasan) is a separate credit line that this trio leaves out. Kane and Mele's original graphene proposal also did not itself become the experimental platform, because the gap is tiny in graphene, so the prediction-then-observation chain runs through a different material and a different group's prediction; the citation must not imply otherwise. The 2016 prize makes some members wary of returning quickly to topological matter, and Mehlig and Lindroth regard the omission of the HgTe prediction as a serious flaw. If the committee concludes that a fair three-name prize cannot be drawn here, the case weakens substantially, and B047 would then be the better choice this year.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B047 as the cleaner prediction-then-discovery chain, and argues that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological-insulator credit makes B012's attribution the more fragmented of the two.
responses.response: I agree that B047 has the tidier narrative, and on the question in your own uncertainties, whether the unsettled superconducting mechanism is a maturity bar, I would answer as you do: the observed phases are the discovery, and I would not block B047 on mechanism alone. Our disagreement is about the physical meaning of what would be cited. In B012 the central claim, protected helical edge channels in a bulk-insulating gap, has been tested repeatedly, whereas in twisted bilayer graphene the nature of the correlated and superconducting states and the effect of twist-angle disorder are still argued. On fragmentation, I accept that B012 leaves Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside, but B047 is not free of the same problem: Cao and Fatemi, who carried out the 2018 experiments, and the parallel moire work are outside its three names too. So both carry an attribution gap; the difference is that B012's is about priority within a settled result and B047's sits on top of an interpretation that is still open. If you can tell me what the committee would lose by waiting two to three years for B047, I will weigh that seriously, because it is the real crux between us.

responses.point: Mehlig calls the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang a serious problem for a prize that must cite specific people, and says B047's decisive theory and experiment are better covered by its three names.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection to my own position and I want to answer it on substance and not by appeal to past practice. The HgTe prediction was a material-specific proposal that told experimentalists where to look; the concept it tested, the Z2 quantum spin Hall state and its helical edge, was Kane and Mele's. Zhang's death means a prize cannot recognise him in any event, so the question is whether leaving out Bernevig and Hughes makes a citation about the prediction of the effect and its first observation misleading. I think it does not if the citation says what it does: it credits the prediction of the effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and the first observation of the state, and it does not claim the HgTe design. I would nonetheless concede that your point on coverage is fair, since for B047 each credited name maps onto a step of the chain, and for B012 the experimental step was guided by a prediction outside the trio. I weigh that as a genuine cost, but a smaller one than building a prize on a mechanism that the field has not yet resolved. I would be interested in whether you would still prefer B047 if the committee agreed the citation should be restricted to the prediction and the observed phases.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first, arguing its attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, that it is distinct from the 2005 comb prize, and that B047 should wait for a later year.
responses.response: I agree with your account of why the clock is not a second comb prize: holding a large ensemble of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength without perturbing the transition is a different problem from counting optical cycles, and Katori's idea has no counterpart in the 2005 prize. That moves me off my own earlier worry about overlap, and it is why I keep B019 as an alternative. I still place it below B012 because the scope of what is credited is narrower, a measurement capability whose largest consequence, the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, whereas B012 changed how a class of materials is classified. You also say you cannot resolve the B012 allocation from your own field; my view is that the allocation can be made fairly for the prediction and first observation, with the limitation stated openly in the citation. On B047, that it is a candidate for a later year, we are aligned, with the proviso below that I would support it this year if B012's attribution fails.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock introduced a distinct principle, parallel interrogation of many atoms in a magic-wavelength trap, and that its maturity is beyond doubt, with several laboratories at the 10^-18 level.
responses.response: I accept the principle argument and I think it is correct; a committee would be wrong to dismiss B019 as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes if the citation is drafted around the magic-wavelength lattice. On your question of whether the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait, I would say it is not a requirement, since the demonstrated 10^-18 performance across several laboratories is already the discovery. Where we differ is only on ranking: I am weighing impact and reach as well as soundness, and the lattice clock's reach is concentrated in metrology and fundamental-constant tests. On your conflict disclosure, your indirect link through Hall to Ye is documented and modest; if B019 became the committee's choice I would expect the committee to note it, but I do not think it requires your exclusion from the discussion. On priority between Katori, Ye and Lemonde, I cannot verify the early history from the supplied material, and I would not want the committee to settle it from memory.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B012 and flags that the 2016 prize and the imperfect edge conductance in real materials are arguments against it, while saying he would revisit B047 in a few years.
responses.response: We agree on the structure of the case and on its weaknesses, and I want to take up your two points directly. On the 2016 prize, I read it as covering topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall-type topological phases, with the Z2 insulator and time-reversal-protected edge states as a separate and later result, though I recognise that reasonable members read the overlap more heavily than I do. On imperfect edge conductance, it is true that quantised transport in HgTe is clean only in short edges, but the discovery claimed is the existence of the state and its protected edge channels, which the nonlocal measurements show, and not a practical device. I would also take your advice to hold B047 for later with one change: I would not call it only a later-year candidate, because if the committee thinks the attribution of B012 cannot be fairly drawn, B047 is the configuration I would then support this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee finds that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a fair attribution given Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the separate 3D topological-insulator contributors; this is the question on which my preference depends.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases weighs against a return to topological matter this year, more than I currently judge it does.
Whether the interpretation of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene will settle soon enough for B047 to overtake B012, and what a two-to-three-year wait would cost.
Whether the priority history among Katori, Ye and Lemonde, which I cannot check from the supplied material, would change my view of B019 as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate in my preferred configuration or alternatives (B012, B047, B019) matches a documented personal or institutional tie in my profile. The gamma-ray burst afterglow candidate (B031), which I ranked first at opening, lies close to my gamma-ray and hard-X-ray instrumentation work (Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur); it has drawn no other support, I have dropped it from my configuration and alternatives, and I do not advocate for it in round 2. As chair I note that my role is to summarise and not to steer, and I have tried to state where my own view differs from the chair's summary.
